segments.speaker: Georgie
segments.text: Hello and welcome to 6 Minute English from BBC Learning English. I'm Georgie.

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: And I'm Neil. Don't forget you can find vocabulary definitions and a worksheet

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: for free on our website bbclearningenglish.com.

segments.speaker: Georgie
segments.text: So Neil, today we're talking about rejection. So, rejection means saying no to someone

segments.speaker: Georgie
segments.text: or refusing to accept their idea or suggestion. Neil, how do you feel about rejection?

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: Well, nobody likes rejection. But I think as you get older, you get used to it. And probably

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: it's quite a good thing to experience rejection, even if it doesn't feel nice.

segments.speaker: Georgie
segments.text: Yeah, I agree. We can't always get what we want, can we?

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: We can't, no.

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: In this podcast, we'll be learning about a new internet trend called rejection therapy

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: and how people are using it to help them to be more confident.

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: OK, let's start with our quiz question, Georgie.

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: Lots of famous people have faced rejection in their lives before they became successful.

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: But which of these things did not happen to the animator Walt Disney before he became successful?

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: Was it A, he lost his job as an artist, B, his first business ran out of money,

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: or C, his first full-length film was a failure?

segments.speaker: Georgie
segments.text: I've got no idea, but I'm going to go with

segments.speaker: Georgie
segments.text: A He lost his job as an artist

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: OK well we find out the answer at the end of the programme

segments.speaker: Georgie
segments.text: OK Neil so most people don like being rejected but one thing to try

segments.speaker: Georgie
segments.text: might be something called rejection therapy.

segments.speaker: Georgie
segments.text: It's a social media trend where people

segments.speaker: Georgie
segments.text: record themselves talking to strangers

segments.speaker: Georgie
segments.text: and sometimes being rejected.

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: OK, that sounds quite interesting,

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: but let's find out how it works in practice.

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: Hannah Gelbart, host of the BBC World Service podcast What in the World, had a go at the trend.

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: Let's see how she got on.

segments.speaker: Hannah Gelbart
segments.text: Can I come sit down at your table?

segments.speaker: Hannah Gelbart
segments.text: Hey, how's it going?

segments.speaker: Hannah Gelbart
segments.text: How's your day gone?

segments.speaker: Hannah Gelbart
segments.text: Good afternoon, how are you doing?

segments.speaker: Hannah Gelbart
segments.text: Can I drive your cab?

segments.speaker: Hannah Gelbart
segments.text: Can I? Can I get behind the wheel?

segments.speaker: Hannah Gelbart
segments.text: Don't be silly.

segments.speaker: Hannah Gelbart
segments.text: Coming somewhere else to try and face my fears.

segments.speaker: Hannah Gelbart
segments.text: Maybe do a bit of shopping.

segments.speaker: Hannah Gelbart
segments.text: I was wondering, can I have a nap in one of these beds? Can I just try it out?

segments.speaker: Hannah Gelbart
segments.text: Wow, I didn't expect that one to be a yes.

segments.speaker: Georgie
segments.text: Well, it seems like people were pretty nice to Hannah in those examples.

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: Yes, and she talked with psychologist Claudia Hammond about how she felt during the experiment.

segments.speaker: Hannah Gelbart
segments.text: And actually walking up to the first person, I felt my adrenaline really, really spiking.

segments.speaker: Hannah Gelbart
segments.text: I'm not a socially anxious person. I think I'm really confident.

segments.speaker: Hannah Gelbart
segments.text: But that first thing really scared me.

segments.speaker: Hannah Gelbart
segments.text: And once I'd done one, the second one came easier and the third one came even easier.

segments.speaker: Hannah Gelbart
segments.text: and, you know, by the fourth time I

segments.speaker: Hannah Gelbart
segments.text: didn't even mind it whether they said

segments.speaker: Hannah Gelbart
segments.text: yes or no.

segments.speaker: Georgie
segments.text: Hannah says that when she walked up to

segments.speaker: Georgie
segments.text: the first stranger in the video she felt her adrenaline spiking If something spikes it increases sharply

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: Hannah is not generally a socially anxious person Someone who is socially anxious is nervous

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: or worried about speaking to other people.

segments.speaker: Georgie
segments.text: Each time Hannah tried to speak to a new person,

segments.speaker: Georgie
segments.text: she says it came easier.

segments.speaker: Georgie
segments.text: Come easier is an informal way to say

segments.speaker: Georgie
segments.text: something is easier to achieve.

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: Now, this social media trend is called

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: rejection therapy, but it's not a proper form of therapy it hasn't been tested.

segments.speaker: Georgie
segments.text: And there are some criticisms of the videos because they involve filming your interactions

segments.speaker: Georgie
segments.text: with strangers, which people might not want.

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: But people who post the videos say they boost their confidence. So why do people want to ask

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: for rejection?

segments.speaker: Georgie
segments.text: Psychologist Claudia Hammond has some ideas,

segments.speaker: Georgie
segments.text: which she shared with Hannah on the BBC World Service podcast, What in the World?

segments.speaker: Georgie
segments.text: What we do know is that there is an increase in perfectionism.

segments.speaker: Georgie
segments.text: People are more worried now, younger people, about how other people are judging them.

segments.speaker: Georgie
segments.text: And so I wonder whether that might make people more shy of speaking to strangers,

segments.speaker: Georgie
segments.text: worried that the people will, you know, not appraise them in a good way.

segments.speaker: Georgie
segments.text: And so doing something like this to try to counter that might feel like a positive step to people that they're trying to do something.

segments.speaker: Georgie
segments.text: Also, they're fun to watch.

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: Claudia says there's an increase in

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: perfectionism among young people.

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: Perfectionism is the feeling that

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: everything you do needs to be perfect.

segments.speaker: Georgie
segments.text: Young people are also worried about how people will appraise them which means judge them

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: Deliberately looking for rejection might be an extreme way to become more confident

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: but it can lead to surprising discoveries.

segments.speaker: Georgie
segments.text: Yes, and Hannah found that most strangers she spoke to were friendly and happy to help,

segments.speaker: Georgie
segments.text: so she didn't really experience rejection much at all.

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: OK, Georgie, I think it's time now for the answer to my quiz question.

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: I asked you which rejection Walt Disney didn't experience before becoming successful.

segments.speaker: Georgie
segments.text: Yes, and I went for A. I don't think he lost his job as an artist.

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: Well, actually, the answer was C. His first full-length film,

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: Snow White and the Seven Dwarfs, was not a failure. It was a huge success.

segments.speaker: Georgie
segments.text: Wow, that was his first film. That's really impressive.

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: It is.

segments.speaker: Georgie
segments.text: OK, let's recap the vocabulary we learned in this programme, starting with rejection,

segments.speaker: Georgie
segments.text: which means saying no or refusing an idea or suggestion.

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: The verb spike means increase suddenly.

segments.speaker: Georgie
segments.text: Someone who is socially anxious is nervous or worried about speaking to other people.

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: If something comes easier, it's easier to achieve.

segments.speaker: Georgie
segments.text: Perfectionism is the feeling that everything you do needs to be perfect.

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: And if you appraise someone, you judge them.

segments.speaker: Georgie
segments.text: Once again, our six minutes are up, but you can test what you've learned with the free worksheet on our website, bbclearningenglish.com.

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: Thank you for joining us and goodbye.

segments.speaker: Georgie
segments.text: Goodbye.
